definitions.type: real Euclidean vector space with measure
definitions.definition: V=R^n, realized as tuples (x_1,...,x_n). Its topology is the Euclidean topology and its measure dx is the product of n one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. Compactness, continuity and derivatives use these topologies; integrable means Lebesgue absolutely integrable.

W=R^m with inner product v·w=sum_{k=1}^m v_k w_k and norm |v|=(sum_{k=1}^m v_k^2)^(1/2). On V the same convention uses n coordinates. The squared norm and dot product in all formulas have this meaning.

u_t(x,r) is the derivative at r of the one-variable map ρ↦u(x,ρ). Derivatives are ordinary Fréchet derivatives in coordinate directions; outside their differentiability set use the total derivative convention zero. This convention grants no differentiability.

definitions.type: family indexed by j=1,...,n of functions V×(0,∞)→W
definitions.definition: u_j(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u(x,r), the coordinate derivative in the jth spatial direction.

definitions.definition: u_jt(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,r). Commutation with ∂_r u_j is a claim to be proved, not part of this definition.
Δu(x,r)=sum_{j=1}^n u_jj(x,r), component by component. The gradient D_x u has columns u_j; its Frobenius square is sum_{j=1}^n |u_j|^2.
e_t(x,r)=∂_r e(x,r), with the total derivative convention of D003.

inputs.statement: For every t0>0 there exist a compact C⊂V and R>0 such that, with J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[−R,R]^n, C⊂(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and every positive-order coordinate partial derivative of u is zero on (V\C)×int J. For each r∈int J the sections of e,e_t,A,B_j,T_j,g_j and ∂_{x_j}g_j (1≤j≤n) are continuous, vanish outside C, have compact support, and are Lebesgue integrable on V. Each is bounded in absolute value on Q and its absolute integral is at most its bound times |Q|. The box Q is compact, measurable, has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞, and C⊂int Q, so all these sections vanish on a neighborhood of ∂Q. In particular e(·,r) is integrable for every r>0.

Let X be a measurable space, μ a measure on X, Z a normed additive commutative group and normed real vector space, I an index type and l a countably generated filter on I. Let Φ:I→X→Z, φ:X→Z and β:X→R. Suppose eventually along l the functions Φ(i,·) are almost everywhere strongly measurable; eventually along l, |Φ(i,z)|≤β(z) for μ-almost every z; β is μ-integrable; and for μ-almost every z, Φ(i,z) tends along l to φ(z). Then ∫_X Φ(i,z) dμ tends along l to ∫_X φ(z) dμ.

argument.text: Fix t0>0. Choose C,R from N002 and use its J=[t0/2,3t0/2], Q=[−R,R]^n. Put η=t0/4>0 and I=[t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J. N003 makes e_t continuous on Q×I. This product is compact, since Q and the closed bounded interval I are compact.
Apply M009 to the continuous scalar function e_t on the compact product Q×I. It gives a real finite bound L for |e_t| on this product.

argument.text: Choose L from F001 and put K=max(L,0)≥0. For 0<|h|<η fix any y∈V. First consider y∈Q and apply M005 to ρ↦e(y,ρ), extended by zero when ρ≤0, on [t0,t0+h] if h>0, and on [t0+h,t0] if h<0. These nondegenerate intervals lie in I, the function is smooth there by N003, and its derivative is e_t with absolute value at most K by F001. The within-interval derivative agrees with the ordinary derivative on these intervals. The resulting estimate is |e(y,t0+h)−e(y,t0)|≤K|h|, hence the absolute quotient is at most K. For y∉Q, both densities are zero by N002, since both times belong to int J. Therefore the quotient is bounded on V by K 1_Q.

produces.statement: For every nonzero ζ with |ζ|<η and every y0∈V, |(e(y0,t0+ζ)−e(y0,t0))/ζ|≤K 1_Q(y0).

argument.text: Define Φ(ζ,y) to be this quotient when 0<|ζ|<η and zero otherwise, and define β=K1_Q. For those small nonzero ζ each quotient is continuous in y, hence strongly measurable, and is integrable as a linear combination of the two integrable density sections supplied by N002. N002 gives measurable Q with finite measure. The nonnegative simple function β has integral K|Q|<∞, so it is integrable. N003 gives pointwise convergence Φ(ζ,y)→e_t(y,t0) as ζ→0 through nonzero values, by the definition of the derivative of e(y,·). F002 is the required domination.

produces.statement: Along the punctured real neighborhood filter at zero, Φ(ζ,·) is eventually strongly measurable and integrable, |Φ(ζ,y)|≤β(y) for all y, β is integrable, and Φ(ζ,y)→e_t(y,t0) for every y∈V.

argument.text: Apply M004 with X=V, μ=dx, Z=R, index set R and the punctured neighborhood filter at zero. This filter is countably generated: the sets {ζ:0<|ζ|<1/k}, k=1,2,..., are a countable neighborhood basis. F003 supplies measurability, domination, integrability of the bound and pointwise, therefore almost-everywhere, convergence. Thus ∫_V Φ(ζ,y)dy tends to ∫_V e_t(y,t0)dy.

For 0<|ζ|<η the two density sections are integrable by N002. M013, applied to e(·,t0+ζ) and −e(·,t0), and M014 with scalars −1 and 1/ζ give ∫_V Φ(ζ,y)dy=(E(t0+ζ)−E(t0))/ζ. Here E is legitimate because N002 proved integrability at every positive time, and t0+ζ>0. Substituting into F004 proves differentiability of the actual energy and E'(t0)=∫_V e_t(y,t0)dy. Generalize over t0>0.
